web_title: 6. 10-Year Financial Forensics, Cash Conversion & Balance Sheet
book_title: Chapter 6: Ten-Year Financial Forensics, Working Capital & Balance Sheet Integrity
question: Do Macpower's 10-year profits convert into real cash flow, why are inventory days at 259, and is the balance sheet built to survive a capex downturn?

epigraph.quote: Revenue is vanity, EBITDA is opinion, but cash flow from operations minus maintenance capex is the only truth a balance sheet cannot fake.
epigraph.author: Forensic Accounting Maxim

web_blocks.html: From FY15 to FY26, Macpower CNC compounded standalone revenue at ~16.2% a year, growing from ₹64 Cr to ₹333 Cr [1]. Operating profit compounded at ~35% from ₹2 Cr to ₹54 Cr, while net profit rose from near-zero to ₹34 Cr [1]. Income statement quality is clean. 'Other Income' was ₹0 Cr in FY26 and ₹1 Cr or less in nine of the last twelve years [1, 3]. Core machine-tool manufacturing drives nearly all reported profit, not treasury or one-off gains [1, 3]. Still, a careful audit must reconcile this strong P&L against weak cash conversion [1, 15].

web_blocks.caption: Macpower CNC: 10-Year Audited Standalone Profit & Loss Statement (₹ Cr, Mar 2017–Mar 2026)
web_blocks.takeaway: Operating margin expanded structurally from 2.4% (FY17) to 16% (FY25–FY26), with near-zero interest expense and a clean ~25%–27% tax rate [1].

web_blocks.caption: Macpower CNC: Standalone Balance Sheet Trajectory (₹ Cr, Mar 2018–Sep 2026)
web_blocks.takeaway: Shareholders' equity compounded from ₹53 Cr (Mar-18) to ₹197 Cr (Sep-26) via retained earnings alone, while borrowings stayed minimal at ₹1–7 Cr [1].

web_blocks.caption: Macpower CNC: 10-Year Cash Flow & CFO/EBITDA Conversion (₹ Cr, Mar 2017–Mar 2026)
web_blocks.takeaway: Pre-tax CFO/EBITDA averaged just 48% in FY26 and 42% in FY25 (cumulative 5-year OCF ~₹36 Cr vs ~₹109 Cr PAT), because rapid top-line growth required heavy inventory absorption [1, 15].

web_blocks.caption: Macpower CNC: 10-Year Working Capital Cycle & Return Ratios (Mar 2017–Mar 2026)
web_blocks.takeaway: Inventory days rose from 184 (FY23) to 259 (FY26), pushing the Cash Conversion Cycle to 182 days—yet ROCE remained exceptional at 27%–30% (FY24–FY26) [1].

web_blocks.html: The core forensic question here is why Inventory Days climbed to 259 days—₹145.6 Cr in March 2026 and ₹170.0 Cr in September 2026 [1, 15, 16]. That buildup stretched the Cash Conversion Cycle (CCC) to 182 days and kept FY26 pre-tax CFO/EBITDA at 48% (₹14 Cr CFO vs ₹54 Cr EBITDA) [1, 15, 16]. Three structural factors drive this stock level [7, 10, 15]. First, Macpower stocks ~20,000 part types across 388+ machine models [7, 10, 15]. Second, management holds up to a year's buffer of imported ball screws, guideways, and controllers to shield delivery schedules from supply shocks [7, 10, 15]. Third, custom defence machines awaiting post-March 15 inspection sit in finished-goods and WIP inventory across fiscal year-end [7, 10, 15].

H1 FY27 offered a live test of whether that working capital is liquid or impaired [15, 16]. Management stopped dispatches against third-party finance-company assurance letters and waited for direct customer or bank funds [15, 16]. That shift cut trade receivables in half, from ₹46.27 Cr in March 2026 to ₹22.89 Cr in September 2026 [15, 16]. As a result, Macpower generated ₹29.97 Cr of Operating Cash Flow in H1 FY27, or ~85% of H1 EBITDA [15, 16]. Cash balances rose to ₹27.20 Cr against just ₹1.58 Cr of debt, leaving ₹25.6 Cr in net cash [15, 16]. Meanwhile, 27%–30% ROCE in FY24–FY26 shows that reinvested capital earns high returns despite the inventory buffer [1]. The key risk is cyclical: if demand stalls while inventory sits at ₹170 Cr, slow-moving WIP would tie up cash for several quarters [15, 16].

web_blocks.title: Forensic Watchlist: Three Balance-Sheet & Cash-Conversion Tests
paragraphs: 1. Inventory Normalization Post-13-Acre Ramp: Inventory Days stood at 259 in FY26 with a 182-day CCC [1, 15]. Both must compress toward <210 inventory days once the 13-acre unit clears floor-space bottlenecks [1, 15].

2. Capex Funding Mix in FY27–FY28: The ₹50 Cr 13-acre plant needs ₹30–40 Cr of FY27 capex [6, 7, 15]. Management plans to fund it with internal cash and subsidized term debt at ~1.25% net interest post-7% state subsidy [6, 7, 15]. Verify that borrowings stay conservative [6, 7, 15].
3. Receivables Discipline: Debtor days stood at 51 days in FY26 and improved in H1 FY27 [1, 15]. Ensure they do not creep back above 60 days as NEXA and government tender shares rise [1, 15].

book_paragraphs: Whenever a manufacturing company shows you 27% revenue growth and a 29% return on capital employed, your first instinct should be admiration—and your second instinct should be to flip immediately to the cash flow statement. Over the past decade, Macpower's income statement has been a model of clean industrial compounding: sales grew from ₹64 crore in FY15 to ₹333 crore in FY26, operating margins stepped up from 2.5% to 16%, and non-operating 'other income' was practically zero. Every rupee of profit came from cutting metal, not from treasury speculation or accounting revaluations.

On the balance sheet, the discipline is equally striking. Shareholders' equity compounded from ₹53 crore at the time of the 2018 IPO to ₹197 crore in September 2026 entirely through retained earnings, with zero fresh equity dilution. Total borrowings stayed negligible—between ₹0 crore and ₹7 crore over the past eight years—even while the company funded ₹9.2 crore, ₹12.4 crore, and ₹15.4 crore of annual capital expenditure across FY24 to FY26 out of internal accruals.

Yet when you and I examine the cash-flow table, a glaring puzzle jumps off the page. In FY26, Macpower earned ₹54 crore in EBITDA and ₹34 crore in net profit, but generated only ₹14 crore in operating cash flow—a 48% pre-tax CFO-to-EBITDA conversion—and just ₹3 crore in free cash flow. Over the five years from FY22 to FY26, cumulative operating cash flow was roughly ₹36 crore against ₹109 crore of cumulative net profit. Where did ₹73 crore of accounting profit go?

It went straight into the stockroom. Inventory days climbed from 184 days in FY23 to 203 days in FY24, 243 days in FY25, and 259 days in FY26—pushing the Cash Conversion Cycle to 182 days. Now, in forensic accounting, rising inventory can mean one of two things: either the company cannot sell its goods (a red flag), or it is deliberately pre-building parts to feed a surging order book (a growth investment). At Macpower, three facts point to the second explanation: it stocks 20,000 part types for 388 models, it deliberately carries a one-year buffer of imported Japanese and German controllers and ball screws to shield delivery timelines, and defence orders completed in late March often sit in finished goods waiting for government inspection.

Still, you should never take management's explanation on faith—you demand proof in cash. And in the first half of FY27, Macpower delivered that proof. By refusing to ship machines against short-term finance-company assurance letters, management cut trade receivables in half—from ₹46.3 crore in March 2026 to ₹22.9 crore in September 2026—and converted roughly 85% of its H1 FY27 EBITDA into ₹29.97 crore of operating cash flow. By September 2026, Macpower held ₹27.2 crore in cash against just ₹1.6 crore of debt, leaving it net cash positive by ₹25.6 crore.

That leaves us with a balanced, clear-eyed forensic verdict. Macpower's balance sheet is fortress-strong, its 27% to 30% ROCE proves that reinvested capital is highly productive, and its H1 FY27 cash surge shows receivables are clean. The one enduring risk is that ₹170 crore of inventory leaves less margin for error if an industrial downturn suddenly slows deliveries, and the upcoming ₹50 crore 13-acre plant investment will test whether management can expand capacity without letting working capital drift higher again.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: On a price-blind basis, Macpower passes our fundamental forensic screen—with one permanent asterisk. A 29% ROCE with net cash of ₹25.6 crore and 16% operating margins is rare in Indian SME capital goods, but 259 inventory days and a 182-day cash conversion cycle mean you must track working-capital discipline every single quarter.
